At 4:17 every morning, the town’s streetlights went out.

No one knew why. The power company said the lights were on timers. The mayor said it was a “minor infrastructure irregularity.” The old woman who lived above the bakery said the darkness was natural and the lights were the mistake.

Mara believed the old woman.

She had begun walking during those four minutes—not because she was brave, but because sleep had become a room with no door. She would put on her coat, step outside, and listen to the town disappear.

In daylight, everything announced itself: delivery trucks coughing at the curb, dogs barking behind fences, the church bell insisting on the hour. But at 4:17, the world loosened. The river stopped pretending to be silver and became simply water. Houses became shapes. The moon, if there was one, looked less like a lantern than a thought someone had nearly forgotten.

On the seventh morning, Mara saw a boy sitting in the middle of the empty street.

He was perhaps eight years old, wearing a yellow raincoat though the sky was clear. In his hands he held a small glass jar. Something inside it pulsed faintly blue.

“Are you lost?” Mara asked.

The boy shook his head.

“Do you live here?”

He shook his head again.

“What’s in the jar?”

This time he looked up. His eyes were the same gray as the river.

“Tomorrow,” he said.

Then the lights flickered back on.

Mara blinked, and the boy was gone. Only the jar remained, resting in the middle of the street. She picked it up. It was warm. Inside, the blue light fluttered against the glass like a trapped moth.

At 4:18, the town returned.

A truck groaned somewhere. A porch light clicked on. Behind a window, someone began making coffee. Mara stood alone beneath the restored lamps, holding the jar close to her chest.

For the first time in months, she felt something move inside her—not hope exactly, but the possibility of it.

She carried the jar home.

And all that day, wherever she went, she could hear tomorrow softly knocking from within.
